verdict.reasoning: Patient says, “It hurts when I pee” and confirms duration: “For six days now… Six days.”
Patient reports, “I've got this sting when I pee.”
Patient notes “Got this very unpleasant smell that comes out,” indicating malodorous urine.
Patient reports tummy pain in the middle; severity “7” and pattern “Comes and goes,” consistent with intermittent mid-abdominal pain rated 7/10.
Doctor asks, “have you actually been able to pass water?” and patient replies “Yes,” indicating ability to urinate is preserved; frequency detail is not given but no impairment is reported.
Patient states, “I've had spotted blood in my urine” and repeats “Yeah, I've had spotting in my urine.”
When asked about temperature/fever, patient says, “No, not at all” and later, “No fever at all.”
Chills are never mentioned or asked about in the transcript; denial of chills is not documented.
Doctor: “have you had any abdominal pain or lower back pain at all?” Patient later confirms, “No, I've got. And no loin pain as well,” indicating denial of low back and loin pain.
Doctor asks, “have you had these symptoms before?” and immediately answers “No, never,” reflecting the patient’s response of no prior similar episodes.
Doctor asks about possible contributors (exercise, dehydration, regular sexual intercourse), and patient answers “No,” indicating no identified recent triggers.
Doctor: “any vaginal discharge or anything like that?” Patient: “No, just the blood spot in my,” denying discharge.
Doctor asks, “Do you have regular periods?” Patient replies, “Yes, I do.”
When asked about past medical problems, patient states, “I had IBS before,” indicating irritable bowel syndrome history.
Doctor asks, “Have you had any problems with your kidneys or any urine infections?” and patient does not report any such history, implying no known prior urinary tract or kidney disorders.
Patient: “I've had Mebavin.” Doctor clarifies, “Do you take that regularly? … do you take it three times a day? … 200 milligrams?” Patient answers “Yes” to each.
On allergy query, patient says “Clindamycin,” and doctor restates, “You are allergic to clindavicin,” confirming clindamycin allergy.
Doctor asks, “anyone in your family had any medical problems?” Patient answers, “No,” indicating negative family history.
Doctor: “Do you live with friends? Family?” Patient: “I live with friends.”
Doctor asks, “Where do you work? What's your job?” Patient replies, “I'm a support worker.”
Doctor: “Do you smoke?” Patient: “No.”
Doctor: “how much in an average week?” Patient: “One glass of wine a week.”
No vital signs or physical exam findings are mentioned anywhere in the transcript; all discussion is history and management.
Doctor states, “It sounds very much like you might have an infection in your urine,” in the context of dysuria, hematuria (spotting), and malodorous urine.

IBS is discussed and when asked, “Any change in your bowel habit, any blood when you pass stool?” patient says “No… Any change in your bowel habit? No,” indicating IBS is without current change in bowel habits.
Doctor: “Normally. We can treat this infection… With a course of antibiotics… It would just be for three days.” Later confirms prescription will go to “Knightsbridge practice” pharmacy for pickup.
Doctor advises, “drink lots of water. So two and a half to three liters a day, you can get some cranberry juice and drink that as well.”

Doctor adds, “also some sachets which you can get from the chemists… which just help change the acidity of your urine. So I can put the details of that on your notes,” consistent with urinary alkalinizer sachets.

Doctor instructs to seek further contact if “your pain is getting worse or not settling, you get lower back pain, or you're getting a high temperature, you have any problems actually passing urine,” which are red-flag symptoms.
Doctor states follow-up is needed if “your symptoms get worse at any point or they're not resolving with the treatment, or you keep getting a similar problem recurrently.”
